comment_text.value:
Software engineers are always responsible for their code except now they have to be responsible for Claude's code

Which is - of course - absurd. Accepting responsibility without demanding the corresponding authority is a fool's game.

I have never been much of an advocate for unionisation in the software development industry. I didn't think it was necessary to protect the interests of the workers because for most of the industry's history the workers have largely been able to stand up for themselves anyway. Likewise I've never been a big believer in accreditation and licensing practitioners in our field - because who is qualified to judge someone else worthy in such a young industry with so little hard data about what works or doesn't work? I find my views on these subjects are evolving now.

It's not about protecting jobs if they truly aren't needed any more or protecting people working in the industry who refuse to move with the times. The Luddite philosophy isn't going to get us anywhere here. And besides - if AI is as effective as its advocates have been claiming then there should soon be more demand for capable developers to take advantage of the new opportunities. (The Jevons Paradox is relevant here.) But it is about protecting standards. If the tools aren't doing a good enough job then expecting professional developers to ship the code produced by those tools even though they know it's junk is something that needs to be challenged. And if developers are being expected to ship anything important without having the slightest idea whether it even works then that's even worse.

We had a lot of silliness going on when the very low interest rates and huge amounts of VC funding were propping up ideas and practices that would never have survived otherwise. Today we have a different kind of funny money distorting the industry but it's still propping up ideas and practices that we wouldn't normally support or perhaps even tolerate. And just like before no individual is going to be able to hold back the tide and it's going to have to be a collective effort to push back - hence my evolving views on topics like unionisation and accreditation. We've all seen the drop in quality across much of the industry and we all know why it's really happening because we see how the sausage is now being made.

I think there's a pretty clear distinction between math and science. The former builds theoretical models of what certain axioms and assumptions imply. The latter builds actual models of what we see and measure in the real world.

Advances in math will probably result in advances in science, which in turn will result in advances in engineering (which is probably where the average person sees an actual benefit in their day to day life). But it's not automatic and a lot of the hand wringing by mathematicians about the AI math results include "is this (AI) method of finding proofs actually going to result in as many of those downstream advances as the old fashioned way?"

(I include theoretical CS as a subfield of math - and believe the S in it is a misnomer).

comment_text.value:
If AI can do what we deem creative work, say implementing a chunk of a Ruby gem, should we still consider such work creative in the first place? I was wondering if we should face an uncomfortable realization: much of what we call being creative was really the cost of overcoming cognitive friction due to the limit of our brains.

Cognitive scientists like Margaret Boden used to break creativity into three different categories: combinatory, exploratory, and transformational. It looks like a lot of our programming tasks are really combinatory and exploratory. Yes, they can be deemed novel and creative by individuals, but collectively they are standardized. It's just like finding integrals used to an art, but nowadays Mathematica can do it better to most of the integrals. Mastering special functions used to be the key to solving tricky PDEs, but nowadays few engineering students need to spend multiple semesters learning them. Quasi-RH was considered a Fields-level hard problem, yet AI could brute-force a proof with elaborate estimates. We humans have a brain that can process only a few variables at a time and it took ingenuity and years of effort to master a series of concepts before using them to solve a problem, but that could be just the cost of knowledge transfer, which AI can drive to zero in many cases.

However, the need for creativity does not go away. It just moves more to the transformational category. In addition, our craft will shift to arguably a less romantic tier: problem formulation, verification, and grounding. It will be a painful transition to many people, me included, but we have no choice but to adapt.

Note I'm not ignoring the economical impact of AI. It's very possible that lowering the cost of producing code increases the aggregate appetite for software, but the demand of software engineers can still go down. Even if total code volume explode tenfold, the labor market may not absorb displaced engineers. I wish there are solutions to this pain, but I fail to see what they are.

comment_text.value:
AI has an incredibly long history of contributing to science and engineering. Some highlights:

Gerard t' Hoofd (under Martinus Veldman) proved in 1971 that Yang-Mills gauge theories are renormalizable, using a rule-based AI (LISP-styled but manually written in assembly) called "Schoonschip" (I'm guessing called that because there were several failed attempts that went before and failed). This program was an AI in the sense of a search algorithm searching symbolic proofs. It got the 1999 Nobel prize in Physics.

This was hugely important because first, it showed that it was possible to make the Standard Model of physics and it also helped beyond that by showing for a lot of (at that point considered) impossible theories exactly how to make them work (meaning not just a proof that it could be done, but a long list of "if you have problem X, do Y" recipes). One of these became first the "electroweak unification", then the standard model.

Hao Wang proved that the logic of "Principia Mathematica" was actually correct using another symbolic proof generator. His efforts were also the start of many other such programs that contributed lots of stuff to mathematics that nobody sane was ever going to do, such as finding all the higher-order versions of the quadratic formula (there's a lot of them).

At Stanford university, tens of thousands of molecules were found in 1965 by having an AI, this one was what's called an "expert system", evaluate mass spectroscopy data and combine it with chemistry knowledge in the form of rules about what was possible or not possible and if only one option remained, spit it out. It almost doubled the sum total of our chemistry knowledge if counted by known molecular structures. It was later adapted to make mass spectroscopy useful in finding the composition of samples.

Then there's Alphafold, first a ConvNet (Resnet+Convnet to be exact), then switched to the transformer architecture, which gave use the folding of just about every protein we have ever found, and even more proteins that we've never even found. Nobel prize in Chemistry 2024.

comment_text.value:
Embodiment for general purpose goals like "grounding, alignment, and AI safety" just seems to be one of those things that some people want to be true. There's no actual reason for it to be true. There are no findings showing it to be true. People just want it to be true anyway.

I'm very skeptical of that. Wishful thinking is a treacherous thing.

LLMs provide some incredibly solid "general purpose commonsense reasoning" primitives. And the likes of Astra, Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 have demonstrated generational leaps in "spatial problem solving" - including robotics tasks. Those don't even have dedicated "sensor input embedding" and "action output diffusion" ends rolled into them at model level - but you can give them control over robot arms, and they'll have a decent chance of, slowly, finding a way to complete new tasks you'd previously would have to tune a robotics model for.

Previously, I have considered "generative video models" to be a decent candidate for the foundation of future robotics models - they, by necessity, perceive video, learn the kind of world dynamics required to plan and execute actions in real world environments. And they can begin to learn those dynamics off embodiment-free general purpose web-scale datasets.

But non-robotics LLM generalists have come to show they're no slouches either. They're not at all optimal for things like rapid precise manipulation. But they find more and more use in robotics pipelines anyway. Makes me wonder what something like "Astra reasoning engine but with robotics architectural extensions" could accomplish.

The tragedy of our predicament - when we are within ideology, is that - when we think that we escape it into our dreams - at that point we are within ideology.

comment_text.value:
There's primary, final, and useful energy. Easy to confuse them. Final is what is delivered for consumption. Useful energy is what is actually delivered in a useful form (motion, light, etc.) The rest is rejected energy (heat). This terminology simplifies a complex chain of events that is about moving and transforming fossil fuels from well (primary energy) via refineries, shipping, trucking, pumping, etc. to gas tank in your car (final energy). After which you burn it to actually get useful energy. There are losses throughout this chain.

The fallacy here is counting barrels of oil, shipments of coal, or whatever and assuming it needs to be replaced 1:1 by what used to be called alternative energy to get the same useful energy. But of course with electrified systems, the losses from generation to use are a lot less. Things like wires and transformers have their own inefficiencies of course. But the numbers are pretty good. You end up with 80-90% useful energy. As opposed to 30-40% for typical fossil fuel plants. And far less for any combustion engine vehicles.

It's called the primary energy fallacy. As Michael Liebreich suggests, there are people using this term that genuinely don't get it. And there are those using it intentionally that do. But the bottom line is that their math tends to be off by about 3-5x.

> Israel needs to exist until Arab countries become developed democracies

A country engaged in genocide needs to exist for your personal benefit? To carry out an obviously failed dream which was sold to the masses as the only viable option to be "safe" from extreme regimes and beliefs?

The West created and supported terrible individuals and dictatorships in the entire region, publicizing them to craft false narratives as a means of controlling the masses, despite it giving these people more power and connections. It's beyond irony that the most dangerous of these threats have roots from direct funding and weapons from the USA/West, while groups and civilians became more organized and extremist directly in response to Western interference over decades. The evidence is clear, modern "wars" are driven by vain political "optics" and individual enrichment. You can't think outside the narrative and rhetoric of these systems and then conclude external action is going to make you safe.

We covertly and overtly mess with their lives, country systems, and leadership. We fund terrorists, criminals, and mercenaries to get our desired result. We invade and fight however we please, insert whoever will benefit us, then retreat on a whim, after destroying the infrastructure and systems of democratic response except for protecting access to what we can take (oil), without a plan for the country or citizens. We leave it to fester, forget the country exists, then later wonder why a country in shock and decline ends up being controlled by violent groups. We then pretend to wonder why the hardened citizens who fought for/with/adjacent/by-proxy for us and lost everything (loved ones, community, home, sense of belonging and safety) suddenly become radicalized. Then we use that as an excuse to start interfering again, or even wipe them out, on repeat. We also respond far harsher to any perceived interference with both hard and soft-power, such as killing civilians (including children), trapped in a country now run by these terrorizing dictators that we either directly supported, trained, or influenced.

By crazy mental gymnastics, many people then believe the conclusion to this is we are clearly superior beings living in the optimal societal system, ignoring the fact that these are humans just like us doing very predictable human things. This gets extended to an extreme belief that we must (and can, and have the right to) eradicate entire groups of people or races and/or re-educate to our way of living. The hyper-rationalizations of our actions to arrive at such flawed logic appears to be a symptom of the system which has been capitalized on for decades; such a complex and abstract atomized society forces us to find a coherent internal narrative that feels safe, aligned, and connected to (the hyper-real) external reality.

Closer to home, our own citizens died in failed wars based on lies, meddling, false-flag operations, scaremongering, and fearful rhetoric. Yet we still believe what we see and fail to question how a lifetime of this leaves us brainwashed into unquestionably feeling superior. It requires active effort to critically question our beliefs in such a system. Those that can't cope watch our own politics and media become extreme, hateful, doomer rhetoric, to be angered into attacking people in our own countries for being slightly different, family even. It's an unnaturally inflated feeling, engineered to heighten the primal fears of anything "other" than what's declared to be correct.

We aren't led by example and we don't have good discussions. Education is to generate workers and self-autonomy, not to provide enlightenment or for personal development. Many never play fair and are praised for it. The past is somehow simultaneously irrelevant and yet paramount, so we are trapped in a loop of exploitation which sucks the life out of culture. We have no vision from the future that doesn't involve despair or escaping the planet. We are at the mercy of "markets" that have no centralized control, planning, or true backups and fail-safes, as the entire system is designed around the idea of self-enrichment rather than human safety and security. Safety nets are illusions or are under threat. Very few seem to know or care.

In the meantime, media institutions, information networks, technology, land, assets, and infrastructure is sold to anyone: designated enemies, adjacent enemies, known terrorists, convicted criminals, dictators, psychologically unsound individuals, etc.

Evidently it's never about making life better for people in the world, never mind in our own countries, and deep down we all know this to an extent. Individualism generates uneasiness from the lack of a primal sense of belonging. We try to mask it constantly with activity and thought, by seeking instant pleasure, ego-massage, and reinforcing our own narratives. Distraction, escapism, and lack of community isn't a model to force on the world. We aren't developed or psychologically sound so much as simply being rich, which allows some self-autonomy - both things we refuse to export anyway as we want money and power. So the whole set of arguments that we are spreading the means of being "stable, civilized, democratic democracy" is absurdly illogical and hypocritical.

Structured systems, open information, and collective action are the foundations of democracy. All have been under constant threat, from dismantling "bureaucracy", attacking access to information and banning/shaming protests to outright murder. With less restrictions and oversight, the scope and scale of power increases, reducing inherent stability and increasing the risk of collapse. The foundational aspects of modern democracy such as freedom of information and communication (without monitoring) is either a farce or constantly under threat.

We have not learned to be critical and aware vs being naive and ignorant, probably because it's scary and highlights how much energy will be required to change. Most choose to instead engage with the controlled reality, which bombards us with crafted actions and media to fuel the primal fear of any "otherness" being a threat, which justifies it to be controlled, exploited, or destroyed. They can then declare to you _why_ you are scared, and how it justifies whatever action that benefits them personally. The outcome doesn't matter to most, anywhere near as much as being told "it was a success" or "we are safer now", "don't worry we have all the answers" etc. Even if we don't believe, we are forced to listen because they hold access to the critical information and means of accessing it to make a decision either way, whilst they actively spread misinformation to deceive us. Our current "democratic" are more rotten and corrupt than the Soviet era.

I'm appalled at the rapid decline of what made the West something I'd recommend and be proud of sharing to developing countries. What we really did was export spying, weapons, technology, information, warfare knowledge, and terrorism. We train and support populations to become militarized, angry, and poor. The shocking state of things is evident and obvious now we have access to so much information. It's becoming less forgivable to ignore the reality hiding under the surface. We only have our ongoing example of society to offer to the world, and from the outside it's a shockingly obscene, hypocritical, primal, self-interested, short-sighted, performative, based hyper-reality that claims to offer personal freedom and federated power, but actually gives corporate freedom, secret alliances rather than competition, and centralized power.

I believe it's the fear of true reality feeds a divide. The primal response to viscerally defend the existing illusions when safety is threatened seems to be strong: double down, ignore all the previous failures, ignore what we can see with our own eyes, ignore the lies and manipulation, believe the false logic, subscribe to a specific way of thinking, and frame arguments about millions of human beings right to exist outside our country through a lens of how it indirectly affects a perceived feeling of safety (and oil prices of course). This happens by giving up a sense of self and becoming part of an invisible system of directed mass psychosis, just like a cult. It's cults, addictions, criminals, and exploitation all the way down. Lucky breaks allow some to struggle less, mostly at the expense of others.

Writing this makes me realize just how screwed up the situation is.

comment_text.value:
I normally don't like talking politics on HN, but as someone who actually worked alongside talented and diligent federal employees I really can't abide this slander. Most of the people I worked with were brilliant and technical people. You think we didn't know we could pull down 2-5× the salary in the private sector? We stayed in the civil service because we were mission-driven and we cared about impacts beyond a quarterly profit motive, even though it paid like shit.

We are talking about people with STEM doctorates and 30 years of experience working 60-80 hour weeks for a 120k salary, because that's about where the GS scale caps. People are on the road for weeks, flying economy class and sleeping in roadside motels with a $50 per diem and when they visit a vendor or a lab or a client they cannot accept a meal or a beer or anything beyond a cup of coffee because of government ethics rules. I worked in an office in Washington, DC where all the staff pooled their money to buy a water cooler, and people gave voluntary donations of $2/month to join the "water cooler club" to defray the cost of maintaining an office water cooler because OPM considered that an unnecessary expense.

The first thing DOGE did, literally in the first week, they implemented a "deferred resignation plan" — they paid people 8 months of salary to not work. The smartest and most talented people saw the writing on the wall at that point — folks with PhDs from MIT or Stanford; self-made founders; crusty veteran engineers who preferred work to retirement. They took the money and they had no problem finding alternative employment, or they took it as a sign to hang up their spurs for good. Many of them were subsequently rehired by their agencies as contractors at 2-3× their previous salary when it became evident they were irreplaceable.

(I had friends in the NNSA, the branch of the US Department of Energy that manages the nuclear arsenal. DOGE fired hundreds of employees without realizing what they did, then attempted to rescind 90% of the firings months later. Plenty of the fired employees had already found new employment. Others simply did not want to return to a job with such contingent status where they would be treated disrespectfully. Several fired employees could not be rehired because they were fired so abruptly there was no way to contact them and offer reinstatement.)

You know who didn't take up the deferred resignation offer? The unproductive layabouts you claim to despise. The ones that knew they couldn't get a better job elsewhere. Yeah, there are bad employees in the federal government, same as anywhere else. DOGE bullied out all our best talent and now we're stuck with the dregs. They paid billions of dollars for people to not work for the privilege of doing so. "Department of Government Efficiency".

If you are interested in learning more about excellent and unglamorous work done by underappreciated American civil servants, I highly recommend the book The Fifth Risk by Michael Lewis.

Modern games look samey because they all want the same result - photorealism - and aren't fussy about using an off-the-shelf solution - i.e. UE5 and Unity. There is some standardization in that, if you issue geometry and sample textures normally, you will be relying on hardware units for rasterization and texture sampling, and those do have a relatively limited set of options for how they work. However, those options encompass most if not all of what 3D engines could ever want or need, even the early 3D ones that had all sorts of hacks. The kinds of things GPUs can't actually rasterize in hardware are things like NURBS or metaballs, but this doesn't matter because the industry settled on triangles[0] as the medium of real-time 3D really early on.

A lot of the look of old 3D games comes down to them doing things the lazy way, and I'm proud to say the lazy way is still very much supported - so long as you turn off features that didn't exist later on and limit yourself. I'm not as familiar with old DOS games, so I'll use the PS1 as an example. The "PS1 look" is very much a result of its incredibly limited rasterizer, whose limitations can be trivially emulated in modern hardware:

1. Don't allocate or bind a depth buffer. You will need to Z-sort your geometry every frame. Part of the "PS1 look" is that some games did it wrong; if you do it correctly you'll be burning performance for no visual benefit. Pick a scheme that breaks in a visually interesting way. Likewise make sure to not allocate any multisampling since the PS1 didn't anti-alias either.

2. Restrict the precision of vertices in your vertex shader by rounding them. The PS1 did vertex math with incredibly low precision and it makes vertices wobble.

3. Restrict the precision of UVs in your fragment shader. PS1 UVs were 0-255, so you want 1/256 precision.

4. Aggressively discard geometry that clips the edge of the viewport. The PS1 did not have proper polygon clipping; you just couldn't render off the end of the viewport, so games had to discard geometry and subdivide polygons to avoid things disappearing. This is another "if you do it well, nobody will notice" thing.

5. Turn off perspective-correct attribute interpolation; this will make your UVs warp and distort at certain angles. You do this with the `noperspective` attribute in GLSL.

6. Disable bilinear filtering when sampling textures.

7. Allocate and render to a low-precision color buffer. Lots of games would change the color depth to match the available VRAM. This is probably the hardest aspect to emulate unless you are actively counting VRAM usage and sticking to realistic values.

8. Bitcrush your textures before uploading them. The same reasoning applies here. Also, don't upload any mipmaps.

9. Lighting was done through vertex colors, which were calculated on the CPU. You don't have to limit yourself to CPU lighting but you do have to make sure lighting is done in the vertex shader.

10. Optional: implement the early model PS1 texture banding bug in your fragment shader.

This will give you a rendering pipeline that is good for basically all purposes except bit-accurate PS1 emulation. Of course, if you were doing bit-accurate emulation, nothing stops you from issuing a screen-filling quad and writing a GPU shader that does software rasterization on the GPU. Or launching a compute shader that accesses the framebuffer arbitrarily - although you do have to worry about memory coherency across warps and workgroups. Texture sampling can also be done "in software" if you so wish - i.e. by doing unfiltered reads to the texture which are glorified array lookups, and then filtering those reads as you wish.

[0] There was a brief moment where quads might have been able to win - artists like to work with them, and Nvidia was shipping quad hardware. But the advantage died very quickly, and quads can be easily converted to triangles - not so much the other way around.

comment_text.value:
> Proving theorems is one of the main ways that mathematicians turn math into money.

Mathematicians working at universities are paid to teach, to engage in the politics and business of government contracting, and only in very rare circumstances to play prestige games on famous problems.

It is unlikely that Congress will decide to slash budget for NSF's MPS directorate on account of AI getting good at proving theorems. That's just not how Congress works.

It is also unlikely that LLMs will be able to do, in the near future, do the sort of applied mathematics that happens in the context of occasional NIH or DoD funding that flows into Mathematics departments, for a variety of complex sociological reasons I'm happy to expound upon.

And it's unlikely Engineering degree programs will stop requiring calculus sequences, since being able to do the computation was has not been the actual point of teaching calc since he late 20th century (if ever).

So, the good news is that I doubt any of this will have much of an effect on the job market for Mathematicians who want to prove theorems for a living. The bad news, of course, is that the job market for Mathematicians who want to prove theorems for a living was already pretty horrendous.

I've been experimenting and building in this space for the past year and wondered the same (repeat founding engineer, MCP and skills.sh OSS contributor, founder @ flocker.md)

Here's what I've tried (and works) for solo/small team dev: - Structured Tasks: LLM's operate extremely well with structured data - try using JSON or YAML for handovers and watch performance level up (genuine Super-Mario mushroom vibes)

- DAG Structures: defining a structured task node <> edge relationship graph can be leveraged directly - great performance boost, particularly for CLI agents, since Claude Opus 4.5

- Task Decomposition: paired with the above, you can easily break down larger epics into smaller tasks - works extremely well for batching, separation of concerns & rapid task delivery

- Task Review Agents: take a decomposed epic, let the distributed work finish, hand the epic definition & completed work over for merge & review - fast, effective

- Agent Identity: this is where things get REALLY interesting (and the space is underdeveloped, building this for consumers @ flocker.md ) - start a chat session by telling the agent what their role is, what it's good at, and load ONLY context useful for the task it needs to do - smaller models suddenly become much more valuable (seriously, try it with GLM Flash 4.7)

- Delegation & Hierarchy: just like people, Agents need authority and delegation channels (with strict bounds) to stay on track - limiting task depth and automated controls seems like the best approach here - delegation feedback loops (effectively task delivery evals) are one of my next implementation tasks for flocker.md (ded)

I've built systems for solo/small teams (let's call them flocks of agents hah) - but thousands of agents would need some seriously well-defined orchestration patterns, and I have yet to see any systems well documented from the big players (probably for good reason).

My genuine guess is it's mostly an (un?)healthy degree of brute force & aggressive culling when isolated context spirals... Let's ask @karpathy: https://x.com/HCJMartin/status/2109963233587015715?s=20

I see Typeface AI have 30-40 people working for them on LinkedIn (some are VC advisors / board members), a lot of them being engineers. Their openings suggest a strong developer market focus (to begin with). I don't necessarily see a lot of people at the company with enterprise sales channel experience, but they already claim to have several Fortune 500 companies as clients (maybe the VCs are helping there or there is natural dev-driven traction).

So they clearly have a product, a strategy around it and perhaps the compliance scaffolding (SOC2 Type II etc) that may be needed before actually being able to charge money for it. They also have the right brand names associated with the founding team. Execution, so far, seems good enough to create a splash, at least.

As an investor, the question(s) to ask is (in my view): "How do they make money? Will that way to make money survive?". The answer to the first: selling input tokens and perhaps subscriptions/credits eventually.The answer to the second: "Yes, but with the risk of unit revenues declining faster than their unit costs". How can they mitigate this problem: by being big (scale / mindshare etc) so that their unit costs (including for customer acq) fall faster than their unit revenues will - I believe that is the question most AI companies are trying to tackle these days. Any new competitor will have to tackle basic fixed costs (of getting started) first before even getting to the stage of having the luxury of worrying about unit-economics.

Hi HN,

This is Yash, founding team at Parseable (https://github.com/parseablehq).

We've built an open source observability data lake using Rust, that handles high-cardinality data at around 100M time series in production (https://www.parseable.com/blog/how-parseable-handles-100-mil...)

Our architecture is built around columnar design, and we use Apache Arrow for in-memory columnar processing and Apache Parquet for durable columnar storage on S3-compatible object storage. In Parseable, every labels stay as columns in the data instead of becoming a large long-lived per-series index like many TSDBs.

Also, one thing we’ve been thinking about a lot is how observability changes as agents become part of day-to-day engineering workflows. They're not just another service, they produce traces, tool calls, prompts, intermediate decisions, errors, costs, and sometimes sensitive business context.

Observing them matters just as much as observing any other system. But it is equally important to decide where that telemetry data should reside. Our view is that teams should be able to keep these observability data close to them: in their own object storage, under their own retention, access, and compliance controls.
